title: How Far Could Stocks Fall?
gist: Jason Furman sizes a possible AI-bubble stock decline: valuation-reversion methods give an 18–41% fall, a 50% drop in the big AI names alone gives 11%, and he picks a 25% baseline (35% bad, 50% severe and very unlikely) while stressing he does not expect a bubble. He argues today differs from 2000 because gains are driven by earnings and a record profit share rather than multiples, and data-center capacity is fully used unlike dark fiber.

insights.claim: Jason Furman's baseline for an AI bubble bursting is a 25% decline in the broad US stock market, with 35% as a bad case and 50% (dot-com scale) as a severe, highly unlikely tail.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Use 25/35/50% equity drawdown scenarios for AI-bust stress tests; 50% is tail-risk only.

insights.so_what: Index concentration means a megacap AI halving alone costs ~11%; contagion would add more.

insights.claim: Jason Furman privately called a Tesla bubble in April 2017 when its market value exceeded Ford's and GM's despite making ~76,000 cars a year versus ~7 million and ~10 million; Tesla has since risen about 1,800%, so it would need to fall ~96% for the call to be right.

insights.so_what: Valuation-based shorts on transformative tech can be catastrophically early.

themes.theme: AI demand vs dot-com dark fiber

insights.claim: Unlike the late-1990s fiber build-out, where by one estimate only 5% of fiber was lit in the early 2000s, today's data-center chips are fully utilized and Nvidia H100 rental prices have risen more than 50% since last December.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: GPU rental pricing is a real-time indicator of AI capex demand; falling rental rates would be an early bust signal.
insights.locator: The demand is also different.

insights.so_what: Commoditization by open-weight models is a key risk to AI-lab monetization and valuations.
